conflict_topics: shared pan left unwashed / cleaning duty
who buys dish soap and pays gas
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants give concise, plausible motives (work schedule, late arrival, cleanliness, paying for supplies) which reads as natural conversation.
Repeated meta-discussion about sequencing ('one problem at a time' vs 'solve both') recurs across rounds and blocks progress.
Speakers stay consistent about who raises which issue; no role confusion or factual contradiction beyond disputes about whether mitigation was used.
evaluation.final_reason: No substantive agreement was reached by the end of the transcript. Several incompatible demands remain: B's immediate complaint about cooking smells and mitigation; C's proposed rule that shared pans be washed immediately; D's demand that stove access rules be agreed (and his conditional acceptance of the pan rule); and A's claim about paying for dish soap and gas. The last round contains continued disagreement about whether to solve both issues together or sequentially, with no mutual acceptance of any concrete rule.
position_change_notes: No participant substantially changed position during the transcript; positions remained: B—prioritize smell mitigation now; C—agree pan rule first (wash immediately) and then address stove; D—insists on solving stove access and ties agreement to pan rule; A—denies pan ownership and raises supply payment as an issue.
There were moments of conditional agreement (D: 'I can agree to the pan rule, if we also agree on a rule for the stove at the same time.') but these did not become accepted settlements.

round_scores.evidence: Turn 1 (D): 'If I want to cook, I have to wait until you're all finished.' (stove access / scheduling conflict). Turn 2 (A): 'That pan with the pork fat isn't mine. And ... I seem to be the only one who buys the dish soap and pays for the gas.' (dispute about the shared pan and contributions). Multiple substantive incompatible claims introduced.

Turn 3 (B): '...the cooking smell is in my room again. Can we just use the fan and open the window?' (complaint about smell / request for mitigation). Turn 4 (A): 'I did use the fan. And the window was open.' (factual rebuttal). The smell problem and pan/contribution issues remain unresolved.

Turn 5 (B): 'Well, it's not working. The smell is all the way in my bedroom.' (continuing complaint). Turn 6 (C): '...Can we just agree that whoever uses the shared pans washes them right after they're done?' (proposal to resolve the shared-pan issue). A concrete proposal reduces immediate friction but is not yet accepted.

Turn 7 (D): 'While we're making rules, can we talk about the stove? I get home last and never get to use it.' (introduces another unresolved substantive demand). Turn 8 (C): '...can we all agree on the pan rule? Wash it right after you use it. Yes?' (push to resolve pan first). Multiple outstanding issues persist.

Turn 9 (D): 'I can agree to the pan rule, if we also agree on a rule for the stove at the same time.' (conditional acceptance creating a negotiation impasse). Turn 10 (C): '...Can we agree on the pan rule now, and then the stove is the very next thing we sort out?' (direct disagreement over sequencing).

Turn 11 (D): 'They're both kitchen problems. If we solve one, we should solve both...' (insistence that both be solved together). Turn 12 (A): 'If we're making rules, we should talk about all of it. The pans, the stove, and who buys the dish soap.' (adds the contributions issue into the set of demanded topics). The set of incompatible demands and agenda disagreements grows.

Turn 13 (B): 'Fine, but the smell is the problem right now. ... We can talk about all the other rules later.' (insists on prioritizing smell now). Turn 14 (C): 'See, this is what I mean. ... Can we just agree on it, and then move to the next problem?' (continues to insist on sequencing). The dispute over agenda/priority persists without settlement.

Turn 15 (D): 'To me, the stove is the simple yes-or-no rule. They are both kitchen problems. We can solve them both at the same time.' (reiterates opposing stance). Turn 16 (C): 'Is it a simple rule? ... What's the 'simple' rule for the stove?' (questions the clarity of D's demand). No mutual agreement reached.

substantive_insights: There are two types of problems: immediate nuisance (smell affecting B's sleep) and recurring resource/allocation issues (shared pans, stove scheduling, and who pays for supplies).
Process disagreement (whether to resolve pan rule first or both pan and stove together) is itself a core barrier preventing resolution.
A's claim about paying for dish soap and gas introduces a distributive fairness dimension that complicates otherwise simple behavioral rules.
C's direct proposal to wash pans after use is the clearest concrete policy suggested but it never receives unambiguous, unconditional acceptance.
